title: {{NAME}} and the Ink That Never Lies
moral: A kingdom built on hidden truths is always one question away from becoming a kingdom built on honest ones.

pages.content: The Kingdom of Arendvale was famous for two things: its archive of royal documents, the largest in the known world, and its Royal Ink, a legendary substance brewed once every hundred years from starflower and moonstone that had the peculiar property of turning invisible whenever it recorded something false. Every treaty, every proclamation, every royal promise, if written in Royal Ink, would fade to nothing the moment a lie tried to use it as a vessel. {{NAME}} was a page in the royal archive, which meant he spent his days filing, cataloguing, and developing the particular kind of eyes that noticed things others missed. He had been summoned by Princess Mira, the king's eldest daughter, who had sharp dark eyes and ink-stained fingers and whose reputation for asking inconvenient questions made the palace courtiers deeply uncomfortable. She met {{NAME}} in the archive's deepest chamber, surrounded by towers of documents, and her expression was not that of a princess seeking assistance. It was the expression of someone who had already found something and needed someone to verify that they weren't imagining it.

pages.content: Princess Mira spread three documents on the table. They were all trade agreements, ancient and official, bearing the great red wax seal of the crown, and they described the terms under which the three hill-villages of Varren had agreed to send half their harvest to the royal city each year. They had been doing so for sixty years. But across a full third of each document, the Royal Ink had vanished. Not faded with age, not smudged, but disappeared entirely, leaving only clean parchment where words had once been written. {{NAME}} bent close, his heart beating faster. He had read about this phenomenon in the archive's own training manual. The ink had not faded because the parchment was old. The ink had faded because what was written there had never been true. Someone had forged royal agreements using Royal Ink, not knowing that the ink would eventually expose them. Princess Mira looked at {{NAME}} steadily. 'The people of Varren have been paying a tithe they never legally agreed to,' she said. 'For sixty years. And someone in this palace knew.'

pages.content: Finding the original documents, the real agreements that preceded the forgeries, required {{NAME}} to climb to the archive's highest and most precarious shelves, a vertiginous series of rolling ladders and narrow catwalks running along the upper stacks where documents from the kingdom's earliest years were stored in numbered cylinders crusted with decades of dust. Princess Mira directed from below, calling out catalogue numbers in a low urgent voice while {{NAME}} pulled cylinder after cylinder, checking and replacing, his arms aching, his boots slipping once on a rung in a way that made his heart lurch sideways. He found them in cylinder forty-seven: the original Varren agreements, written in a different hand, in ordinary ink that had not vanished at all, because it told the truth. The villages had agreed to send a tenth of their harvest, not a half. Not a tithe that left families hungry every winter, but a fair exchange that left everyone comfortable. He tucked the documents under his arm and descended, and the look on Princess Mira's face when she saw them was worth every bruise.

pages.content: The royal council chamber felt enormous and cold when Princess Mira presented the documents, {{NAME}} standing beside her as a formal witness, trying not to fidget with the brass buttons on his coat. Lord Pemberton, the royal treasurer, went the colour of old milk. He had been the archive-master sixty years ago. He was very old and very proud and very still as Mira laid the two sets of documents side by side and the council members bent over them in silence. The king, {{NAME}} noticed, looked not angry but enormously, painfully tired, the way people look when something they half suspected but had never examined finally becomes impossible to ignore. Princess Mira did not shout or accuse. She simply placed the documents where everyone could see them and waited, with a patience that seemed to fill the room like warm light. The truth, {{NAME}} was learning, did not need an advocate. It only needed space to breathe.

pages.content: The correction was announced within the week. The Varren villages would receive sixty years of overpayment returned, a figure that made even the royal treasurer wince, and the original agreement would be honoured going forward. {{NAME}} learned about it not in the council chamber but in the archive, where he was quietly refiling the documents into their proper cylinder, the real ones at the front and the forgeries behind them as evidence, properly catalogued for the first time. Princess Mira stopped by on her way to the feast being held in the Varren ambassadors' honour, wearing a gown the colour of deep blue water, and she paused at the archive door and looked at {{NAME}} with an expression he would remember for a long time. 'Archives are usually where secrets go to hide,' she said. 'You helped make this one a place where secrets come to be found.' He went home through the palace's candlelit corridors feeling as though his feet barely touched the stone, warm and full of rightness. His candle burned low as he curled into bed, and he was nearly asleep when he noticed, tucked under his door, a small scroll sealed with silver wax he had never seen before.
